title: System Design Interview Framework
oneLine: Control the interview: clarify scope, estimate scale, draw the main flow, then spend the remaining time on the riskiest decisions.
opening: I use a four-step structure. First, I clarify users, core workflows, scale, consistency, latency, and failure expectations so we solve the intended problem. Second, I define APIs, the main data model, rough estimates, and a high-level architecture. Third, I select two or three deep dives based on the system’s real risks—such as ordering, partitioning, idempotency, hot keys, or reconciliation. Finally, I summarize trade-offs, bottlenecks, observability, security, and how the design evolves. I keep checking for interviewer buy-in instead of presenting a memorized architecture.
ask: Which user journeys are in scope and explicitly out of scope?
What scale and latency target should drive the design?
Which data invariants require strong consistency?
Which two deep-dive areas would be most valuable to discuss?
scale: Typical 45-minute allocation: 5–8 min scope and estimates, 10–15 min high level, 15–20 min deep dives, 3–5 min wrap-up.
Aim for two or three deep dives, not shallow coverage of ten technologies.
Reserve time to revisit assumptions and identify the next bottleneck.

decisions.default: Get a coherent end-to-end design first, then go deep on the highest-risk components.
decisions.why: A perfect cache discussion cannot rescue a missing write path or invariant.
decisions.switch: Go deep earlier when the interviewer explicitly anchors on one subsystem.

decisions.default: Describe required properties before naming a product.
decisions.why: It demonstrates architectural reasoning and avoids technology-by-association.
decisions.switch: Name concrete options to show implementation credibility after the property is clear.

decisions.default: State and record them visibly; revise when the interviewer changes scope.
decisions.why: Most poor answers solve a different problem than the one asked.
decisions.switch: Use a reasonable default when information is unavailable, but label it as an assumption.

deepDives.title: A strong diagram
points: Separate synchronous critical path from asynchronous side effects.
Show ownership of state and where ordering/transactions occur.
Draw external dependencies and failure boundaries, not only boxes.

deepDives.title: Data first
points: Name primary entities and access patterns before selecting storage.
Identify uniqueness, ordering, balance, inventory, or permission invariants.
State partition key and lifecycle/retention for large records.

deepDives.title: Finish like an architect
points: Call out hotspots, consistency, security, observability, rollout, and cost.
State what you deliberately did not build yet.
Describe the first evolution step at 10× scale.

failures.response: Time-box clarification and estimates, get buy-in, and explicitly choose the top deep dives.
Keep a small assumptions panel and refer back to it when making trade-offs.
Walk one read and one write end to end, including retries and source of truth.
Start with the smallest design that meets the stated scale; explain the trigger for the next mechanism.

questions.q: What should I do when the interviewer is silent?
questions.a: State the assumption you will use, explain why it is reasonable, and proceed. Periodically offer a choice of deep dives instead of asking open-ended permission at every step.
Only when a network partition or replicated write path makes the consistency/availability trade-off relevant. Name the concrete user-visible behavior rather than dropping the acronym.
Enough to expose idempotency, pagination/cursors, filtering, async status, and core resource boundaries. Do not spend the interview writing a full OpenAPI specification.

questions.q: How do I sound senior rather than memorized?
questions.a: Tie choices to invariants, operational reality, migrations, and failure behavior. State alternatives and the condition under which you would choose them.

mistakes: Beginning with Kafka, Redis, and Kubernetes before defining the problem
Ignoring write paths and only describing reads
Claiming exactly-once or zero downtime without a mechanism
Failing to summarize the design and unresolved risks
seniorSignal: Own the conversation. Convert ambiguity into assumptions, make decision criteria explicit, and spend time where correctness or scale is genuinely hard.
implementation: Practice drawing the same visual grammar: edge, stateless compute, state, log/queue, workers, observability
Prepare concise examples from your capital-markets systems for latency, entitlement, failure isolation, and migration trade-offs
Use concrete implementation anchors only after explaining the architectural property
